intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Knobloch syndrome-2 (KNO2) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the PAK2 gene (605022) on chromosome 3q29.

checks.claim: Knobloch syndrome-2 (KNO2) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the PAK2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We conclude that the KNO2 syndrome in the studied family is dominant and caused by a deleterious variant in the PAK2 gene.
checks.explanation: The abstract describes the variant as monoallelic, which means heterozygous.

checks.claim: The PAK2 gene is located on chromosome 3q29.
checks.evidence_quote: Dominant monoallelic variant in the PAK2 gene causes Knobloch syndrome type 2.
checks.explanation: The chromosomal location is standard nomenclature added to a gene the paper names, so it counts as supported under the rules.

paragraphs.text: Menzel et al. (2004) described Knobloch syndrome as a disorder characterized by high myopia, vitreoretinal degeneration with retinal detachment, and congenital encephalocele. Antonarakis et al. (2021) studied a family they designated KNO2, with Knobloch type 2 syndrome with intellectual disability, autistic behavior, retinal degeneration, and encephalocele.

paragraphs.text: Menzel et al. (2004) described Knobloch syndrome as autosomal recessive. In contrast, Antonarakis et al. (2021) concluded that KNO2 in the family they studied was dominant. They found a heterozygous variant that was apparently de novo in both affected sibs. This indicated likely germline mosaicism in one of the parents, although deep sequencing of parental blood DNA did not detect mosaicism.

paragraphs.text: Menzel et al. (2004) analyzed 2 unrelated Knobloch syndrome families, from Hungary and New Zealand. They confirmed that COL18A1 is involved in the disorder and showed that it is genetically heterogeneous. Linkage to the COL18A1 locus was excluded in the New Zealand family, which provided evidence for a second Knobloch syndrome locus. They named this locus KNO2.

paragraphs.text: Antonarakis et al. (2021) performed whole-exome sequencing in a family with KNO2, including the 2 affected sibs and their normal parents. They identified a heterozygous glu435-to-lys (E435K) mutation in the PAK2 gene as the causative variant. The mutation was apparently de novo in both sibs, indicating likely germline mosaicism in one of the parents, but deep sequencing of parental blood DNA did not detect mosaicism. The mutation lies in the kinase domain. Structural analysis predicted that it might compromise kinase activity, and in transfected HEK293T cells it caused a partial loss of kinase activity.

paragraphs.text: Antonarakis et al. (2021) used whole-exome sequencing to study a family with Knobloch syndrome-2 (KNO2), in which 2 sibs had intellectual disability, autistic behavior, retinal degeneration, and encephalocele. Both sibs carried a heterozygous glu435-to-lys (E435K) mutation in the PAK2 gene. The mutation was apparently de novo in both sibs, suggesting germline mosaicism in a parent, but deep sequencing of parental blood DNA did not detect mosaicism. The mutation is in the kinase domain. Structural analysis predicted that it might compromise kinase activity, and in transfected HEK293T cells it caused a partial loss of kinase activity.
